name: Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga)
autonymMeaning: evokes food taboos linked to meat
overview: In the majority in Meiganga, where they live alongside the Toupouri, Bororo, Bamiléké and Hausa, the Baya (Bouforo) belong to the large Gbaya group that extends from Sudan and the Central African Republic to the Congo and Nigeria. An egalitarian society yet attached to respect, they grow cassava, maize, potato, beans and yam, and the labi school, a genuine training of warriors, remains at the heart of their education.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority and dominant group, in contact with the Toupouri, Bororo, Bamiléké and Hausa; many also speak Fulfulde, English or a Bamiléké language.
Baya is spoken in Sudan, the Central African Republic, Congo-Brazzaville, Nigeria and in the East of Cameroon (Bertoua, Bétaré-Oya, Batouri).
In the chiefdom, people marry among the Baya; in the community, exogamy is widely accepted, especially for men.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The Fulani lamido arrived first; the founding grandfather came from Lorta to Meiganga, where the neighbourhood was born in 1935.
Gonga means “the truth” in Baya, a name given by a Fulani.
The Baya, who came from Sudan via Nigeria and the Central African Republic, still receive visits from Sudanese relatives.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Egalitarian society, based on mutual respect between elders and juniors; the chiefdom, however, forms a world apart.
The chief decides with 17 notables, each responsible for a block.
The inheritance stays within the clan.
Relations between unmarried people of both sexes are forbidden; modesty is expected, and the young respect the elders.
Marriages and alliances link the Baya to their neighbours.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the woman leaves her family for her husband's.
One comes of age around 18; one marries around 25 for a man, 18 for a woman if she does not continue school.
The girl's consent is needed first, and she indicates which relative to go and see; her family then investigates the suitor, whose conduct matters above all.
The bride price consists of one arrow and one hundred francs, kept in the grandfather's trunk as a symbol of life; the suitor may afterwards, of his own accord, help feed the in-laws.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Ancestor cults every year, at births and in times of epidemic.
Sacred places in the forest, at home or in town, kept secret.
Birth is a reincarnation; death, the return to God.
Many taboos and prohibitions: incest is a very serious offence; one does not befriend a stranger without the elders' advice.
Capital offences: cohabitation outside marriage, stealing, killing, lying, and not paying one's debts, which remain owed even after death.
An elder of the tribe can gather the children and guess for them.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men and women: farming (cassava, maize, sweet potato, beans, yam) and trade.
The land belongs to the Gbaya, but the State is its first owner; it is accessed through the lamido and the sub-prefect.
Crafts: fish trap (ngen), clay pot for the chiefdom's water.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Plaited clothing bakoa and kofia; moenam, garment of the Gbaya association; formerly, dried skins for women.
Medicine based on barks and leaves is declining.
Beauty is work and above all honesty; to attract someone, one must first be clean, elegance comes after.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: gbaza (large and small drums) for adults, rerengué for children, mbamenga (warriors' dance), ladi.
People also dance for an appointment or a success at school.
Festivals: harvests, Christmas, New Year.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The labi school, comparable to military training, is essential in the life of the Baya.

sections.title: The names
items: Baya names are recognisable by their sound.
Among Muslims, kola nuts and biscuits are offered and the imam blesses the child; non-Muslims hold a christening. The name does not change.
One does not call someone by their real name; terms of respect: metè (child), ènètè (elder).
The ancestor is called Godanwa Bawé.

lessons.competence: Introduce the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority and dominant group, in contact with the Toupouri, Bororo, Bamiléké and Haoussa; many also speak fulfulde, English or a Bamiléké language. • Baya is spoken in Sudan, the Central African Republic, Congo-Brazzaville, Nigeria and the East of Cameroon (Bertoua, Bétaré-Oya, Batouri). • In the chiefdom, people marry among the Baya; in the community, exogamy is widely accepted, especially for men. • The Fulani lamido arrived first; the founding grandfather came from Lorta to Meiganga, where the neighbourhood came into being in 1935. • Gonga means “the truth” in Baya, a name given by a Fulani.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority in Meiganga, where they live alongside the Toupouri, Bororo, Bamiléké and Hausa, the Baya (Bouforo) belong to the large Gbaya group that extends from Sudan and the Central African Republic to the Congo and Nigeria. An egalitarian society yet attached to respect, they grow cassava, maize, potato, beans and yam, and the labi school, a genuine training of warriors, remains at the heart of their education.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

steps.instruction: Among the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga), traditional dances (gbaza, rerengué, mbamenga) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: large and small drums. Festival(s): harvest festival, Christmas and New Year.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men and women: farming (cassava, maize, sweet potato, beans, yam) and trade. • Land belongs to the Gbaya, but the State is its first owner; access is through the lamido and the sub-prefect. • Crafts: fishing trap (ngen), canari for the chiefdom's water.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.langText: lieux secrets en forêt et à la maison
amitié avec un étranger sans l'avis des anciens

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Worship of the ancestors every year, at births and in times of epidemic. • Sacred places in the forest, at home or in town, kept secret. • Birth is a reincarnation; death, the return to God. • Many taboos and prohibitions: incest is a very serious offence; one does not befriend a stranger without the elders' opinion. • Capital offences: cohabitation outside marriage, stealing, killing, lying, and not paying one's debts, which remain owed even after death.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Ancestor cults every year, at births and in times of epidemic. Sacred places in the forest, at home or in town, kept secret.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.memo: Ancestor cults every year, at births and in times of epidemic. Sacred places in the forest, at home or in town, kept secret.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Gbaya
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Gbaya. • Greeting formulae: Mewozme = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Mosane = morning greeting (one person); Mosame = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Pkok, Hito, Ta’a, Moro, Pok. • The ancestor is called Godanwa Bawé. • The labi school, comparable to military training, is essential in the life of the Baya.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Gbaya are the first steps towards communicating with the Baya (Bouforo, Meiganga). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
